title: The spacecraft, or the sensors?
task: Open what each reading depends on, keep what stands alone, and name what the rest share.
scene: Nine minutes after the bang, three cabin pressure readings fall together. A mechanical gauge and a leak listener are also live. The flight director wants one answer before the crew opens any panels.
assumes: several instruments can run off one shared circuit
a reading that stands alone does not inherit that circuit's fault
takeaway: Several readouts agreeing count as one, when they all hang off the same thing.
question: Which pressure evidence survives, and what moved the rest?
why: Agreement is only strong evidence when the things agreeing could have failed separately. These three digital readings share one circuit. Shift that circuit and all three move together, whether or not the cabin does. The mechanical gauge works a different way altogether, and it has not moved. The leak listener hears nothing. So three frightening numbers turn into one electrical fault, and the evidence that still stands is kept rather than thrown out with them.
answerText: Keep the mechanical gauge and the leak listener. The three digital channels share one circuit, and that circuit is what moved.

title: Build the first picture
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to happen.
scene: Three consoles hold numbers that disagree. One power bus reads zero. The guidance computer has restarted with no memory of what it saw. Nothing has been written down yet.
assumes: a number without its units and its time is not a measurement
takeaway: An answer built to survive being wrong has to be built in a particular order.
why: The recordings from across the failure get wiped within minutes, so they are saved before anything is worked out. Units and clocks come next. A tidy answer built from mixed clocks is confidently wrong. Then the estimates, each with a range rather than one number. A number with no range cannot be argued with. And the only commands worth sending are the ones that help whatever turns out to be true.

cards: Save the recordings from before and after the failure.
Check the units, the clocks and what each reading depends on.
Work out where it is, how it is moving and how it is doing, each with a range.
Send only the commands that help whatever the truth turns out to be.
rebuttals: Save the recordings first. It is the only step with a deadline set by a machine rather than by people.
Units and clocks second. This is where one shared fault shows up, instead of being fitted into the answer.
Estimates third, each with a range. A single number cannot be argued with or tested.
Commands last, and only the ones that survive every answer the data still allows.

title: Spend the first ten minutes
task: Say what the flight director does first.
scene: Four controllers, a crew in a spacecraft that is venting something, and ten minutes to the next tracking pass. Every desk believes its own problem is the one that kills them.
assumes: two rooms acting on different versions of one number is worse than either acting alone
takeaway: Attention is a resource in an emergency, and the first decision is where it goes.
question: Ten minutes to the next tracking pass. What does the flight director do first?
why: Attention runs out like fuel does. Four people are already working the same failure from four sets of numbers, and nothing says which set is the real one. One log and one voice giving commands stops the same work being done twice and contradicted once. Organising the room is not a delay before the technical work. It is what makes every later calculation count once instead of three times.
answerText: Open one log and name one person to give commands. Everything after that counts once instead of three times.

choices: Open one log, and name one person to give commands.
Rebuild the timeline of the power and the pressure.
Check the trajectory and the attitude independently.
Ask every desk for a full report at once.
rebuttals: The power and pressure timeline is the first real piece of work, and the log is what holds it. Start it second and it survives the shift change.
Checking the trajectory decides whether they can get home. It is needed before the burn, not before the room is sorted out.
Six full reports arrive after the tracking pass, and eat the ten minutes that were meant to prepare for it.

title: Which measurement gives what
task: Match each thing you need to know to the measurement that gives it.
scene: The onboard computer has restarted and the tracking comes and goes. The room has to rebuild where the spacecraft is from whatever can still be measured, and say what each measurement buys.
assumes: saying where something is and how it is moving takes more than one number
takeaway: No single measurement gives a position. Each one gives a piece, and the pieces are different shapes.
why: Each measurement answers a different question and none of them answers all of it. Photographing the spacecraft against known stars gives a direction and no distance. Timing a radio pulse out and back gives a distance and no direction. The pitch of the returning signal says how fast it is coming or going, and nothing about sideways motion. And rates come from repeating: two positions give a speed, two speeds give a change in speed.

scenarios: How fast it is coming toward us.
choices: Photograph it against stars whose places are already known.
Compare the pitch of the signal coming back with the one sent out.
Time a radio pulse out to it and back again.
Measure the same thing twice, and subtract.
rebuttals: Direction is an angle, and the star camera is the only instrument here that measures one.
Motion toward us or away shows up in the pitch of what comes back, and nowhere else.
A distance is a speed multiplied by a time, which is what the round trip gives you.
Rates come from repeating. Two positions give a speed, and two speeds give a change.

title: Rebuild where it is
task: Put the four steps in order.
scene: The computer restarted and lost its bearings. A distance, two angles and a pitch trace remain, recorded on different clocks. The next tracking pass will test whatever the room reconstructs.
assumes: measurements only combine when they are on the same map and the same clock
takeaway: A useful answer predicts the next measurement, and says how sure it is.
why: Everything goes onto one map and one clock first, or a tidy answer comes out wrong in a way nobody can see. The distance, the angles and the pitch then get fitted together. Each pins down something different, and fitted apart they give three answers. What the fit misses is read for pattern rather than size. A pattern is a force nobody allowed for. Then it is carried forward to the burn.

cards: Put every measurement on one map and one clock.
Fit a path that matches the distance, the angles and the pitch together.
Look at what the fit misses, and see whether the misses form a pattern.
Carry the answer, and its range, forward to the hour of the burn.
rebuttals: One map and one clock first. Two clocks in one fit is the mistake that never shows up afterwards.
Fit all three together second. Fitted separately they give three answers and no way to choose.
Read the misses third, for pattern rather than size. A pattern is a force nobody modelled.
Carry it forward last. The burn happens later than the measurements, and the doubt grows on the way.

title: What holds it in the curve
task: Say why the spacecraft needs speed to stay in that path.
scene: The return path swings the spacecraft round the Moon at two and a half thousand kilometres up. Somebody on the loop has asked why it does not simply fall onto the surface.
assumes: something moving in a circle is being pulled toward the middle, even at a steady speed
takeaway: An orbit is falling, with enough sideways speed that the ground keeps curving away.
question: Why does the spacecraft need any speed at all to stay in that path?
why: It is falling. It has been falling the whole way round. What stops it arriving is sideways speed: while gravity pulls it down, it moves along, and the Moon's surface curves away underneath at about the same rate. Too slow and the path meets the ground. Too fast and it swings out and away. Nothing is holding it up, which is exactly why the crew float. Falling and floating are the same thing here.
answerText: It is falling the whole way round. Its sideways speed means the surface curves away as fast as it drops.

choices: Its sideways speed turns constant falling into a curve around the Moon.
An outward force balances gravity, so nothing is pulling it anywhere.
Its speed weakens the Moon's pull on it.
Its forward motion holds it up, the way a wing holds up a plane.
rebuttals: There is no outward force. The spacecraft is being pulled inward the whole time, which is what bends the path.
Speed does not weaken gravity. It changes the shape of the path that gravity produces.
There is no air out there to push against, and the engine is off for nearly all of it.

title: How a spacecraft turns
task: Match each change to what it does to the turning.
scene: The guidance computer is out and the crew is about to fly by hand. Before anybody touches a thruster, the room says plainly what each change does.
assumes: a push off to one side is what makes something start or stop turning
takeaway: Turning follows the same rules as moving. It is just harder to see them.
why: Four rules cover every hand-flown turn. The same push further from the middle turns harder, which is the one the crew can actually choose. The same push on a heavier, more spread-out craft turns it more slowly, and stops it more slowly too. A push one way and an equal push back cancels out, which is what starting and stopping a turn actually is. And moving things about inside changes nothing overall, because nothing inside can push on the outside.

scenarios: The same push, further from the middle.
The same push, on a craft that is harder to turn.
An equal push one way, then the other, for equal times.
Moving things about inside, with nothing pushing from outside.
choices: It turns harder.
It turns more slowly.
The turning cancels out, and it ends up as it started.
The total turning cannot change, however things move inside.
rebuttals: The same push further out has more leverage, and it is the term the crew can actually choose.
The same push on something harder to turn gives less turning. Harder to start, and just as hard to stop.
Equal pushes for equal times cancel out. That is exactly what a start pulse and a stop pulse are.
Moving mass inside shifts the turning about between parts, and it cannot change the total.

title: Turning it by hand
task: Choose the opening pulse and where to start braking, then run the turn.
scene: The guidance computer is off. The crew has to turn the spacecraft ninety degrees using two thruster pairs and a mark on the window. Every extra correction spends fuel meant for the return.
assumes: a push changes how fast something turns
it keeps turning after the thruster stops
takeaway: Stopping the push does not stop the motion, so the braking has to start early.
question: How hard do you start the turn, and where do you start braking so it arrives still?
why: A thruster pulse does not make a turn that stops itself. It changes how fast the spacecraft is turning, and when the pulse ends it keeps going at that rate. Stopping needs the opposite thruster, and that takes just as long as starting did. So the braking has to begin before the target, by about the angle the starting pulse used up. Brake at the target and it sails past. The turn only works if the angle and the turning both reach zero together.
answerText: Brake before the target. A six-second pulse gets it turning at twelve degrees a second, which takes about thirty-six degrees to stop, so braking starts near fifty-four.

title: Turning effect from a thruster
task: Work out the turning effect of the thruster.
scene: A thruster pushes with two hundred newtons, three metres out from the middle of the spacecraft. The crew needs the turning effect before it can predict how fast the turn starts.
assumes: the same push further from the middle turns something harder
takeaway: Where a push is applied matters as much as how hard it pushes.
question: How much turning effect does the thruster give?
why: Turning effect is the push multiplied by how far out it acts. Two hundred newtons, three metres from the middle, is six hundred. Move the same thruster in to half the distance and the turning effect halves, with the same fuel burnt. That is why the crew care which pair fires. They cannot make the thruster stronger, and they can choose one that acts further out, and it is exactly the same amount of fuel either way.
answerText: Six hundred. Two hundred newtons pushing three metres out from the middle.

estimate.prompt: The thruster pushes with 200 newtons, at right angles, three metres out from the middle of the spacecraft.
estimate.question: How much turning effect does the thruster give?
estimate.relationship: Turning effect = the push × how far out it acts.
estimate.explanation: The distance has to be measured to the middle of the spacecraft, not to whatever piece of structure is nearest. The mass of the craft decides how fast it then turns, and it is not part of this sum.
labels: 3 m (how far out the thruster is)

title: How long can the battery last?
task: Turn the store and the draw into hours.
scene: The fuel cells are gone, and the crew is on the entry batteries days earlier than any plan allowed. The flight surgeon wants a number of hours before the next decision about switching things off.
assumes: a store is an amount, and a draw is how fast it is being used
takeaway: An amount divided by a rate is a time, and that time is what every other decision gets argued against.
question: How long will the batteries last?
why: There is a store and there is a draw, and dividing one by the other gives hours. Eighteen kilowatt hours at three kilowatts is six hours. It is an ideal figure. It assumes the draw stays flat and that every last bit of the store is usable, and neither is quite true. A cold battery gives less than its label. It is still the number every argument this shift is measured against, so it is worth having early and worth calling rough.
answerText: About six hours, if the draw stays flat. It is a rough number, and everything today gets argued against it.

estimate.prompt: The entry batteries hold about 18 kilowatt hours that can actually be used. The things that must stay on draw about 3 kilowatts.
estimate.question: How long will the batteries last?
estimate.relationship: Hours = what is in the store ÷ how fast it is being used.
estimate.explanation: The bus voltage says how the energy is delivered, and nothing about how much there is. The time to the next burn is a deadline rather than an ingredient.
labels: 18 kWh (what is usable in the batteries)

title: Why is the voltage sagging?
task: Say which fault fits the voltage, the current and the heat together.
scene: The power bus is sagging at twenty-four volts instead of twenty-eight, while the total current sits where it was planned to be. Engineers want to start pulling equipment off.
assumes: current pushing through something that resists it drops the voltage and makes heat
takeaway: Voltage, current and heat are three views of one fault, and one view is not enough.
question: Which fault fits the voltage, the current and the heat?
why: Three readings, one fault, and each says something different. Something extra drawing power would show up as more current than planned. The current is where it should be. A failed supply would show as less coming in, and what comes in is normal. What is left is something in the path resisting. It eats voltage going past and turns it into heat.
answerText: A bad connection in the path. It eats voltage on the way through and turns it into heat, which is why the joint is warm.

choices: A bad connection somewhere in the path.
Something extra drawing power that nobody knows about.
The supply itself has failed.
Only the voltmeter is wrong.
choiceMechanisms: A resisting joint drops the voltage past it, and turns what it drops into heat.
An unexpected device pulls extra current and drags the bus down.
Less is coming in, so the battery has to make up the difference.
The bus is fine, and only one instrument is telling a story.
rebuttals: Something extra drawing power would show as more current than planned, and the current is where it should be.
A failed supply would show as less coming in. What is coming in is normal, so the fault is further along.
A bad voltmeter explains the reading and not the hot joint or the extra battery current. Two instruments agree.
text.headline: The power bus sags under a load that is exactly what was planned.

title: Switch things off without losing the mission
task: Share out the amp-hours, and keep every needed condition met.
scene: Forty-one amp-hours left, and sixty-two hours to fly. Guidance, radio, heating and life support all want power. Something has to be turned down within minutes.
assumes: an amp-hour is a current drawn for an hour
some things can be switched on and off, and some cannot
takeaway: A power budget is not a ranking of what matters. It is hours multiplied by draw, and the total is fixed.
question: How many hours of each can the spacecraft afford?
why: This is not a list of what matters most. It is a sum. Every load costs its draw multiplied by the hours it runs, and the total cannot pass forty-one. Life support runs the whole way, so it is bought first. Guidance is needed in fixed windows, so those get booked. Heating can be switched on and off, and not removed, because a cold battery gives less back.
answerText: Buy life support for the whole return. Book the guidance windows. Keep enough heating to protect the batteries. What is left pays for short radio windows.

title: How much does the cabin cool?
task: Work out how far the temperature falls in three hours.
scene: With most things switched off, the cabin is losing about a kilowatt more heat than it makes. The flight surgeon wants to know how long the crew has before the cold becomes a medical problem.
assumes: it takes energy to warm something up, and the same energy leaves as it cools
takeaway: Big things change temperature slowly, and that slowness is time to think.
question: How far does the cabin cool over three hours?
why: The cabin and everything in it is heavy, and heavy things take a lot of energy to warm or cool by even one degree. A kilowatt leaking for three hours sounds alarming, and against this much stuff it is under a degree. That is the useful part. The cold is real and it is slow, so the crew has hours rather than minutes. The same fact is why warming it back up later costs so much.
answerText: Under one degree. The cabin is heavy, so a kilowatt leaking for three hours barely moves it.

estimate.prompt: The cabin is losing about 1,000 watts more than it makes, for three hours — which is 10,800 seconds. Warming this cabin by one degree takes about 12 million joules.
estimate.question: How far does the cabin cool over three hours?
estimate.relationship: Degrees lost = energy lost ÷ energy for one degree. Energy lost = watts × seconds.
estimate.explanation: A watt is a joule every second, so the time has to be in seconds. Use hours instead and the answer is out by three thousand six hundred.
estimate.solution: 1,000 × 10,800 is 10.8 million joules. Divided by 12 million, that is about 0.9 of a degree.
labels: 3 h (the same three hours, in hours)

title: How the heat is getting out
task: Match each thing happening in the cabin to how the heat is moving.
scene: The cabin is cooling and the crew wants to do something about it. What they can do depends on how the heat is actually leaving, so the room names the route first.
assumes: heat moves by touching, by riding on moving air, or by beaming across a gap
takeaway: Naming the route is what tells you which fix would work at all.
why: Heat leaves three ways, and each has a different fix. By touching, which needs contact and is short range. By riding on moving air, which is why circulation spreads warmth about. And by beaming straight across a gap, which needs nothing in between and works fine in vacuum. A metal strut running out to the cold structure is the worst kind, because it touches all the way and never stops. Insulation, circulation and shiny surfaces each work on a different one.

scenarios: Moving air carries warmth round the cabin.
A cold wall soaks up warmth from everything facing it.
A metal strut runs out to the structure outside.
choices: Heat moving by touching.
Heat riding on moving air.
Heat beaming across a gap.
Heat conducted straight out along metal.
rebuttals: People in contact pass heat by touching. It is short range and it needs contact.
Air carrying warmth about the cabin is heat riding on something moving, rather than passing through it.
A cold wall soaking up warmth from across the cabin is heat beaming across a gap. It needs nothing in between.
A metal strut to the outside conducts all the way out, and it never stops. That is the leak that runs all night.
columns: What is happening in the cabin

title: Keep the cabin survivable
task: Say what the last of the energy should be spent on.
scene: The cabin is at four degrees and falling. Water is beading on the walls and the crew is sleeping in their suits. Heating all of it is not affordable on what is left.
assumes: slowing a loss and replacing it are different things
takeaway: Slowing a loss keeps paying. Replacing it has to be paid again every time.
question: Four degrees and falling, on a fixed amount of energy. What do you spend it on?
why: There are two ways to fight cold and they cost differently. Replacing heat means paying again the moment you stop. Slowing the loss keeps working after the spending stops, which is what matters when the energy is fixed. So it goes round the crew and round the batteries, where cold does the most damage. Cold batteries also give back less than warm ones, so a heat problem quietly becomes a power problem if nobody attends to it.
answerText: Wrap the crew area and the batteries. Slowing the loss keeps paying after the energy is gone; reheating has to be paid for again every time.

choices: Wrap the crew area and the batteries, to slow the loss.
Spend the rest on short bursts of heating the whole cabin.
Run the fans all the time, so everywhere is the same temperature.
Heat the electronics bay, and let the crew rely on their suits.
rebuttals: Reheating the whole cabin replaces what has gone and does nothing about the next hour. The same energy gets spent again.
Running the fans evens the temperature out and costs power the whole time, and it does not slow anything leaving.
Protecting the electronics keeps the hardware and lets the crew and the batteries go on cooling.

title: Follow the air
task: Build the air path in order, then name the link that is holding it up.
scene: Carbon dioxide keeps climbing. The scrubber fan sounds normal and draws its usual current, and the airflow is low. There are pressure readings on both sides of the filter.
assumes: a motor running does not prove any air is moving
air has to pass through every part of a loop
takeaway: A chain moves at the rate of its most restricted link, not the rate of its noisiest one.
question: Where does the air path become the problem?
why: The fan makes a push. How much air moves depends on everything downstream of it. Normal current only proves the fan has power. The pressure difference across the filter is large and the flow is small, which is what a blockage looks like. Every breath has to get through that filter before it reaches anything that cleans it. So the loop runs at whatever the filter allows.
answerText: The filter. The fan is fine, and almost nothing is getting past that filter, so nothing reaches the scrubber.

title: How much they breathe out
task: Work out how much carbon dioxide the crew makes in six hours.
scene: Three crew, each breathing out about twenty litres of carbon dioxide an hour. The workshop needs to know what a home-made scrubber has to keep up with over the next six hours.
assumes: a rate multiplied by a time gives a total
takeaway: The rate something arrives at sets the smallest rate that can remove it.
question: How much carbon dioxide do they make in six hours?
why: Three people at twenty litres an hour make sixty litres an hour between them. Six hours of that is three hundred and sixty. That number is the bar. Anything that removes carbon dioxide more slowly than the crew makes it does not hold the level steady. It only makes the rise slower. The workshop does not need this precise. It needs to know whether what they can build is big enough to matter at all.
answerText: About 360 litres. Sixty litres an hour between the three of them, for six hours.

estimate.prompt: Three crew each breathe out about twenty litres of carbon dioxide an hour, and the scrubber has to keep up for six hours.
estimate.question: How much carbon dioxide do they make in six hours?
estimate.relationship: Total = what one person makes an hour × how many people × how many hours.
estimate.explanation: A rate for one person needs a head count and a stretch of time, and both have to match the question. The daily figure describes the same crew and cannot be used here without more work.

title: Make the air breathable
task: Say what the improvised fix has to get right.
scene: Carbon dioxide is close to the limit and still climbing. The spare canisters are square, the socket is round, and there is tape, a suit hose, a sock and a plastic cover.
assumes: air, like water, goes the easiest way it is offered
takeaway: Nothing gets cleaned unless it goes through the thing that cleans it.
question: Tape, a hose, a sock and a plastic cover. What does the fix have to get right?
why: Two things have to be true, and only one of them is obvious. There has to be something that takes the carbon dioxide out, and every bit of air has to be made to go through it. Air is lazy. Leave a gap round the canister and most of it goes round instead of through, and comes back into the cabin exactly as it left. A big canister with a gap round it cleans less than a small one taped tight.
answerText: A sealed path, so the air has nowhere to go but through. A gap round the canister undoes everything else.

choices: A sealed path, so the air has to go through the canister.
As much of the canister exposed to the cabin as possible.
Readings taken in several places round the cabin.
A fan loud enough that the crew can hear it running.
rebuttals: Exposing more of it only helps the air that reaches it. A big canister with a gap round it cleans less than a small one taped tight.
Measuring in several places is how they find out whether it worked. That is necessary and it is not the fix.
A fan they can hear proves a motor is turning. It says nothing about how much air is moving, or where it goes.

title: Why did the signal fade?
task: Change one thing at a time, and put it back, until the fade follows something.
scene: Voice and data have gone weak at two ground stations at once. The spacecraft's transmitter is putting out what it should. Three things can be swapped without risking anything.
assumes: a fair test changes one thing and leaves the rest alone
takeaway: A cause is proved when the effect follows the change both ways.
question: Which change makes the fade appear and disappear?
why: Several things can weaken a radio link, and only one test settles which. Swap to a different ground receiver and nothing changes, so it is not one receiver. Swap the transmitter chain and nothing changes, so it is not the transmitter. Correct where the antenna is pointing and almost all the missing signal comes back. Point it wrong again and the fade returns. Following the change in both directions is what makes it a cause rather than a coincidence.
answerText: Where the antenna is pointing. Correcting it brings the signal back, and putting the error back makes it fade again. Neither swap changes anything.

title: How long is one wave
task: Work out how long one wave of the radio signal is.
scene: The link is fading, and the antenna team needs the length of one wave for its pointing model. The spacecraft transmits two billion waves a second.
assumes: radio travels at a fixed speed, three hundred million metres every second
takeaway: How long a wave is decides how fussy the aiming has to be.
question: How long is one wave?
why: Radio covers three hundred million metres in a second. In that same second, two billion waves go past. So one wave is that distance shared between them, which is about fifteen centimetres. The number matters because the dish sends its signal in a beam. Short waves make a narrow beam. A narrow beam reaches further, and it has to be aimed far more carefully.
answerText: About fifteen centimetres. That short a wave makes a narrow beam, which is why the aiming has to be so exact.

estimate.prompt: Radio travels 300 million metres each second, and this signal fits 2 billion waves into that second.
estimate.question: How long is one wave?
estimate.relationship: Length of one wave = how far it travels in a second ÷ how many waves fit in that second.
estimate.explanation: Read the big numbers carefully. Millions instead of billions makes each wave a hundred and fifty metres long, which would need an aerial nobody could fly.
labels: 300,000,000 m each second (how fast radio goes)
2,000,000 waves each second (the same figure, misread)
343 m each second (the speed of sound)

title: Get the link back
task: Put the four moves in order.
scene: The signal is weak and drifting. The crew is answering calls it can barely hear. The next navigation update depends on getting the link back.
assumes: a slower message needs less signal to be read
takeaway: Do the biggest and cheapest thing first, and let each move buy the next.
why: Pointing is the biggest thing on the list and the cheapest to fix, so it goes first. Slowing the message down comes next. Less is being sent, so less signal is needed to read it, and nothing aboard has to change. Then the big ground dishes get told where to listen, because the signal has drifted. What comes back feeds the navigation the burn needs.

cards: Check where the spacecraft is pointing.
Slow the message down, and listen over a narrower range.
Point the big ground dishes, and tell them where to listen.
Feed the tracking that comes back into the navigation.
rebuttals: Pointing first. It is the biggest term in the sum, and the cheapest one to fix.
Slowing the message down second. A slower message needs less signal, and it costs nothing aboard.
The big dishes third, told where to listen, because the signal has drifted in frequency.
Navigation last. Getting the link back also produces the measurements the burn needs.

title: What is shaking it?
task: Say which explanation fits how the shaking depends on speed.
scene: A bad vibration only appears when the wheel runs near one speed. Above and below that it dies away. Two sensors on different parts of the structure see the same narrow band.
assumes: everything has speeds at which it prefers to shake
takeaway: What matters is not how hard it shakes, but what is shaking it, and how fast.
question: Which explanation fits the readings?
why: Everything has a rhythm it likes to shake at, the way a swing does. Push a swing at any old moment and little happens. Push it in time with itself and it goes higher every push. Here the wheel is the push, and one speed lands in time with the structure's own rhythm. Move off that speed either way and the pushes fall out of step. That is why the vibration has a narrow band rather than growing with speed.
answerText: The wheel is pushing in time with the structure's own rhythm. That is why it only happens in a narrow band of speed.

choices: The wheel is pushing in time with the structure's own rhythm.
One sensor has come loose and is rattling.
Something hit it once, and this is the after-effect.
The structure is breaking up.
choiceMechanisms: A repeated push lands in time with the structure's rhythm, and the shaking builds.
One sensor rattles on its own mount while the structure is quiet.
A single knock rings the structure, whatever the wheel is doing.
Damage shakes everything, at all speeds and all frequencies.
rebuttals: A loose sensor rattles on its own mount. A second sensor somewhere else sees exactly the same thing.
A single knock does not care what speed the wheel is running at, and nothing recorded an impact.
Breaking up shakes at every speed. This is narrow, repeatable, and it stops when the speed changes.
text.headline: A bad vibration appears only in a narrow band of wheel speed.

title: How far to stay clear
task: Work out the highest speed that is safely below the bad band.
scene: The bad band runs from three thousand one hundred to three thousand three hundred turns a minute. The rule is to stay two hundred clear of it, and the pump still has to run.
assumes: a shaking problem has a band of speeds, with room either side
takeaway: Avoiding a resonance is arithmetic on the band, not a matter of running gently.
question: What is the highest speed that is safely below the band?
why: A resonance is a band rather than a point, and a margin either side of it is what stops the pump wandering back in. The band starts at three thousand one hundred. Two hundred clear of that is two thousand nine hundred, and that is the fastest the pump can safely run below it. Running slower is fine. Running anywhere between three thousand one hundred and three thousand three hundred is not, and neither is sitting just outside and drifting.
answerText: Two thousand nine hundred turns a minute. The band starts at 3,100, and the rule is 200 clear of it.

estimate.prompt: The bad band runs from 3,100 to 3,300 turns a minute. The rule is to stay 200 clear of it.
estimate.question: What is the highest speed that is safely below the band?
estimate.relationship: Highest safe speed = the bottom of the band − the clearance.
estimate.explanation: Work off the bottom of the band, not the worst point in the middle of it. Using 3,200 puts the pump inside the band it is meant to avoid.

title: Stop the shaking
task: Say what the safest immediate move is.
scene: A panel shakes whenever the pump runs near one speed, and it has grown worse over three cycles. The pump is needed, and its speed can still be changed from the panel.
assumes: shaking like this needs a structure and something pushing it in time
takeaway: Change what is pushing, when you cannot change what is being pushed.
question: What is the safest immediate move?
why: This kind of shaking needs two things: a structure with a rhythm, and something pushing in time with it. In flight, changing what is pushing is far easier than changing the structure. Moving the pump speed off the band stops the pushes landing in time, and it can be undone in a second. Deadening the panel is the proper permanent fix, and it needs hardware and somebody's hands on it. Running faster through the band assumes it survives the crossing.
answerText: Move the pump speed off the band. It stops the pushes landing in time, and it can be undone at once.

choices: Move the pump's speed away from the band.
Deaden the panel, so the shaking dies away.
Measure it in a few more places first.
Run the pump harder, to get through the band quickly.
rebuttals: Deadening it bleeds the energy away and is the right permanent fix. It needs hardware, access and somebody's hands on the structure.
Measuring in more places is how you check the fix worked. It is the check rather than the fix.
Getting through quickly assumes the structure survives the crossing, which is exactly what three growing cycles have called into question.

title: Really off course, or one bad clock?
task: Say which explanation fits all four checks.
scene: Several ground measurements suddenly put the spacecraft ahead of where it should be. They agree with each other. A star camera and the clock records are both available.
assumes: several instruments can be wrong together if they share a part
takeaway: When measurements agree, ask whether they agree separately or share a part.
question: Which explanation fits all four checks?
why: Agreement counts only when the things agreeing could have failed apart. These measurements all use the same ground clock, so one clock error moves them together. The star camera does not use that clock, and it still matches the prediction. Nothing pushed the spacecraft, and the onboard readings show no push either. Redo the sums with the corrected clock and nearly all the error disappears. Several agreeing numbers turned out to be one fault.
answerText: One shared clock. The measurements that moved all use it, and the star camera, which does not, still agrees with the prediction.

choices: The spacecraft really is off course.
One shared clock is wrong, and it moved everything that uses it.
Several instruments failed separately, at the same time.
The star camera has failed.
choiceMechanisms: It has actually moved away from the predicted path.
One shared timestamp shifts everything worked out from it, together.
Unrelated instruments happen to drift the same way at the same moment.
The star camera alone is producing a wrong answer.
rebuttals: Moving off course needs a push, and the onboard readings show no push at all.
Separate failures do not drift the same way at the same moment. These share a clock.
A failed star camera would put its answer in the wrong place. It is the one that agrees with the prediction.
text.headline: Several ground measurements suddenly put the spacecraft ahead of where it should be.

title: How much room is left
task: Work out how much clear space is left either side.
scene: The entry corridor is forty kilometres wide. The circle of doubt around the spacecraft's position is ten kilometres across. Sandoval needs a margin before the burn is called.
assumes: a position is the middle of a circle of doubt, not a fact
takeaway: A route is planned against the doubt, not against the line drawn through the middle of it.
question: How much clear space is left on each side, if it flies down the middle?
why: The corridor is forty kilometres wide, so aiming down the middle puts twenty either side. The spacecraft could be five kilometres off in any direction, so five of those twenty are already spent before anybody makes a mistake. Fifteen is what is left. That is the number the burn is judged against, and it is why the doubt has to be drawn at the same scale as the corridor rather than mentioned in a footnote.
answerText: Fifteen kilometres each side. Twenty from the middle of the corridor, less five for how far off the spacecraft might be.

estimate.prompt: The corridor is 40 kilometres wide. The circle of doubt around the position is 10 kilometres across.
estimate.question: How much clear space is left on each side, if it flies down the middle?
estimate.relationship: Margin = half the corridor − half the doubt.
estimate.explanation: Both get halved, because both are widths and the spacecraft is aiming down the middle of them. Take the whole doubt off one side and the answer is too gloomy by five kilometres.
estimate.solution: 40 ÷ 2 is 20. 10 ÷ 2 is 5. Twenty take away five is 15 kilometres.

title: Burn, or look again?
task: Spend the last of the tracking on what could change the decision.
scene: Two tracking answers disagree, and both lean on the same station clock. A correction burn is ready to go. There is time for one more piece of evidence before the decision closes.
assumes: two measurements that share a clock are not two pieces of evidence
a rougher measurement can be worth more than a precise one
takeaway: The measurement worth buying is the one that could fail differently.
question: Which evidence is worth buying before committing the burn?
why: More precision on the same clock cannot settle a question about that clock. Redoing the sums makes the numbers tidier and leaves the clock exactly where it was. Another pass tied to the same clock has the same weakness. A star-camera sighting uses different physics and a different reference altogether, so it can say whether the spacecraft has actually moved. When there is time for one thing, being different matters more than being precise.
answerText: Buy the star-camera sighting. It is the only one that could disagree with the clock, which is what the argument is about.

title: What still needs checking
task: Spend the two checks on the claims where being wrong costs most.
scene: Eleven minutes to entry. Four signed statements sit on the flight director's console. Some have real measurements behind them and one does not. Two checks can still be done.
assumes: a signature records who is responsible, not whether it is true
time to check should go where being wrong costs most
takeaway: A signature says somebody believes it. The evidence behind it is a separate question.
question: Which claims deserve the last checks before the radio goes quiet?
why: Paper readiness and real readiness are different things. Three of these have direct measurements behind them: tracking, a known correction, a checked setting. The heat shield changed and the record of the change is incomplete, and it is also the one where being wrong ends the flight. So one check goes there. The second confirms the entry path is still inside the corridor, because that is the other thing nobody can fix once the radio stops.
answerText: Check the heat shield first, then that the path is still inside the corridor. The other two already have measurements behind them.

title: The order the silence forces
task: Put the entry steps in order around the four minutes of silence.
scene: Everything now depends on eleven minutes, and four of them have no radio at all. Anything that needs the ground has to happen before the silence starts.
assumes: nothing can be fixed from the ground while the radio is quiet
takeaway: When part of a plan cannot be changed, everything that might need changing goes before it.
why: Four minutes of silence sets the whole order. Anything that needs a decision from the ground has to be settled first, because during the silence there is nobody to ask. Who is flying gets agreed before the silence, not during it. Watching the slowing and the heating can only start once entry has begun, so it comes after. And the recording runs throughout, because this flight is the only test the predictions will ever get.

cards: Set the approved attitude and settings, because none of it can be changed during the silence.
Agree who is flying, before the radio goes quiet rather than during it.
Watch the slowing and the heating against what was predicted.
Come down, and keep the record of what actually happened.
rebuttals: Attitude and settings first, before entry. Nothing here can be changed through four minutes of silence.
Agree who is flying before committing. That is not something to work out while nobody can talk.
Watching the slowing comes third. It cannot start before entry, because there is nothing to compare yet.
Descent last, with the record kept. This is the only flight that will ever produce this data.

title: What the review should fix
task: Say which proposal removes the cause rather than improving the response.
scene: The crew is aboard the recovery ship and the review board meets Monday. Four proposals compete for three funded places.
assumes: a fix that removes a cause outlasts a fix that improves the response
takeaway: Fixing what caused it outlasts getting better at coping with it.
question: Which proposal deserves first place, because it removes the cause?
why: The same weakness appeared twice on this flight. Three pressure readings shared one circuit, and later several tracking numbers shared one clock. Both times, agreement looked far stronger than it was, and both times somebody nearly acted on it. Removing those shared parts is the only proposal that stops it happening again. Keeping better records and rehearsing more both help people cope with it, which is a different and smaller thing.
answerText: Remove the shared parts. Everything else on the list helps people cope with the same failure rather than preventing it.

choices: Redesign the shared circuits and shared clocks, so agreement means something.
Keep the full records of telemetry, settings and decisions.
Improve the simulator, and rehearse failures more.
Put more people on the anomaly desk for future flights.
rebuttals: Keeping the records is how anybody reconstructs it afterwards, and it leaves the shared parts exactly where they are.
Rehearsing improves how people handle the same failure. It does not stop the shared clock failing again.
More people can diagnose it faster, and the shared part is still there to fail.
